newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serb students in all-night rally, police withdraw.
newsitem.headline: Serb students in all-night rally, police withdraw.

text.p: About 3,000 Serbian students, blowing whistles and cheering "Victory", marched through the streets of Belgrade early on Saturday when police withdrew after an all-night stand-off.

"This is proof that the police and the government cannot destroy the protests," Tedomir Jovanovic, a student protest leader, said after students began marching when the police withdrew at 6:30 a.m (0530 GMT).
"They can only make the students stop if they give us what they want," a weary but elated Jovanovic said.
The cordon of 300 riot police, plus more in buses, left Belgrade's Terazije Square after preventing the students from marching an hour after midnight as they have for the past few nights.
The students, who had dwindled to about 1,000 but quickly grew in numbers, then marched through the pre-dawn streets yelling "Wake up Belgrade" and "Let's go for a walk".
The students are supporting demands by the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition for the reinstatement of the results of annulled November municipal elections.
Zajedno candidates won 14 of Serbia's biggest cities but President Slobodan Milosevic and the ruling Socialists have so far thwarted efforts to reinstate the opposition victories.

It was the first time that there has been an all-night stand-off between police and students, but the mood throughout the night was mostly friendly. At one point, priests sprinkled the police cordon with holy water.
"The government wants to send us home but they must realise that after 60 days (of protests) our home is on the streets until they give us what we want," Jovanovic said.

Vuk Draskovic, a Zajedno leader, has called for a mass demonstration of people in uniforms later on Saturday to try to drum up flagging support for the daily demonstrations across Serbia, now into their 62nd day.

"Tomorrow we must stage a mass protest to mark these two months (of protests) and face the police in our own uniforms --- army reserve, civil defence, doctors, stewardesses, every possible uniform," Draskovic said on Friday.

With numbers of demonstrators down sharply to a daily average of 15,000 to 20,000 in Belgrade, opposition leaders said it was time for another big rally approaching in size the half million who turned out on Orthodox New Year.

The opposition said on Friday that a court in Serbia's second-biggest city of Nis had rejected a Socialist Party (SPS) challenge to an electoral commission ruling restoring the opposition's victory there.
"The court ruled that the Socialist Party's appeal was unfounded," Zoran Zivkovic, the local Zajedno leader, said by telephone on Friday.
Earlier this week, electoral commissions in Nis and Belgrade ruled that the opposition victories there were valid.

But Ratko Markovic, a Belgrade University law professor and member of the SPS executive board, said in a statement read on state-run Serbian television that the reasoning behind the electoral commission decisions was deeply flawed.
Markovic said electoral commissions had no legal authority to overturn court decisions, and therefore the court rulings which threw out the Zajedno victories for "irregularities" remained in effect.
"All in all, the decision of the municipal electoral commission is a nightmare of legal nonsense, illegalities and fallacies," Markovic said in the statement read during the evening news broadcast.

"It's as if someone went to pains to put everything upside down -- the administration controls the legality of the court...The decision is thus a legal monstrosity that could only have been thought up by someone who wanted to ridicule the law."

Socialist hardliners have vowed to challenge the pro-opposition ruling in Belgrade, snubbing a plea from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) to concede electoral defeat in the 14 cities.

But the persistent mass demonstrations by Zajedno and allied university students have rattled the foundations of the left's effective one-party rule stretching back to 1945 and brought international celebrity to the opposition leaders.
